dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: ELIS provides an adjacent professional-services comparator that reinforces the cluster’s selective-deployment and work-redesign thesis. It reports operational gains among AI implementers while showing that organisational capability to integrate new roles remains weak; however, its perception-based, language-industry evidence does not directly establish effects in legal work.
qs: Up to half of the companies which implement AI themselves report a positive effect, through higher efficiencies, lower costs or additional service offerings.

A majority of the participating companies,                                                          however, are not aware of the existence of                                                          these roles or have no idea how to integrate                                                          them in their operations.

st.t: Translation work: Automation erodes autonomy unevenly
st.an: ELIS 2025 supports the proposition by reporting that technology-driven substitution is reshaping surviving translation work through reduced volumes, price pressure and discounted post-editing, producing substantial insecurity among freelancers. It also supports the cluster’s emphasis on uneven effects by distinguishing severe pressure on independents and small companies from stronger outcomes in larger, interpreting and audiovisual segments.
qs: Stronger price pressure, especially from large language companies, a drop in work volume and the generalised move from human translation to discounted and less-valued post-editing make 53% of the participants question their future as a freelance professional.
According to third-party research however, the larger international LSCs are suffering less.

kp.k: Survey findings chiefly represent European freelancers and smaller companies
kp.d: ELIS 2025 comprises five surveys with 1322 participants from 50 countries: 654 independent professionals, 179 language companies, 71 language departments, 137 university staff and 281 students. Among company respondents, 88% represented businesses with revenue below €5 million. The report explicitly treats answers as participants’ opinions and expectations, not objectively verified data; country response thresholds were reached for companies in 11 countries and independent professionals in 18. Its findings concern language services rather than legal practice generally.
qs: ELIS 2025 consists of 5 separate surveys tuned to the needs and interests of each industry segment.
Users of this report need to keep in mind that the data are not objective and verifiable.
ELIS participants mainly represent the European market of small and medium sized LSCs and independent language professionals.

kp.k: Reported contraction is concentrated among smaller language providers
kp.d: For 2024, 50% of language-company respondents reported decreases or strong decreases, averaging 19%; the 18% reporting increases averaged 16% growth. All represented size segments below €10 million reported average revenue decreases. For 2025, providers expected their own activity broadly to stagnate, with net expectations of −2% for companies and +2% for individuals. A small net majority of companies expected global and local markets to shrink for the first time. These expectations differ from reported 2024 outcomes and are not forecasts established by independent measurement.
qs: 50% language company respondents reported a decrease or strong decrease, on average by 19%. The 18% that still experienced an increase reported an average increase by 16%.
All ELIS size segments below € 10 million report an average decrease of revenue in 2024.
For the first time a (small) net majority of language companies expect both of them to shrink in 2025.

kp.k: Providers predominantly attribute declining activity to structural technological change
kp.d: The report says 77% of company participants attributed declining activity to structural industry changes, principally language-technology adoption and altered client procurement. Another 14% expected a return to normal, while 9% attributed losses to external economic or geopolitical factors. Respondents associate AI and dedicated machine translation with reduced outsourcing, price pressure and substitution of discounted post-editing for human translation; these are participant attributions rather than a causal identification of AI’s effects.
qs: 77% of the LSC participants believe that the decline in activity is caused by structural changes in the industry itself
Both independent professionals and language companies link the trend directly to indiscriminate use by clients, loss of quality and appreciation, and increased price pressure.

In line with the trend remarks, language companies primarily report a direct negative impact of AI on their business, either by clients reducing their outsourcing or as a result of the reduced rates for post-editing.

kp.k: Machine translation now covers roughly half of professional projects
kp.d: Reported company machine-translation use increased by 1000 basis points to 50% of handled projects; the report gives 54% for independent professionals. Company AI use was reported at 34%. Although overall machine-translation implementation stagnated, actual use increased. Generative AI was the exception to otherwise non-increasing technology implementation, and was used for translation, editing, quality control, research and content creation.
qs: Actual MT use by language companies has increased by 1000 BP and reaches now the magic mark of 50% of handled projects. AI makes its entry with an impressive 34%.
Even with a stagnating implementation level of MT, its actual use in terms of number of projects has significantly increased, although university staff and students continue to overestimate it.
Generative AI is most often used as an alternative for machine translation (less so among language departments) or for editing and translation quality control.

kp.k: Freelancers increasingly initiate machine-translation use themselves
kp.d: Client-pretranslated projects remained at 24%. The share of professionals voluntarily using machine translation rose from 58% in 2024 to 69%, while respondents using it in at least half their projects increased from 16% to 29%. The report finds no direct correlation between voluntary use and overall activity change; it suggests that associations at the extremes may reflect professional attitudes rather than a technology effect.
qs: The percentage of projects that are pre-translated by the client (predominantly language companies) has remained unchanged at 24%.
Both the number of professionals who make this choice (69% vs 58% in 2024) and the number of respondents who use it in 50% or more of their projects (29% vs 16% in 2024) are increasing significantly.
There is no direct correlation between voluntary use of MT and the overall activity increase or decrease

kp.k: AI implementation benefits coexist with market-level losses
kp.d: Up to half of companies implementing AI reported benefits through efficiency, reduced costs or additional services, but 28% reported no significant effect and some reported negative effects. In trend comments, 23% of companies recognised AI’s efficiency potential, compared with only 13% of independent professionals mentioning AI or machine translation as a positive development. Smaller companies were more critical than larger respondents.
qs: Up to half of the companies which implement AI themselves report a positive effect, through higher efficiencies, lower costs or additional service offerings.
Interestingly, 28% do not see any significant impact after implementation.
Only 13% mention these technologies (also) as a positive development.

kp.k: Post-editing expands within a contracting and repricing market
kp.d: Normalised company revenue shares rose by 700 basis points to 27% for post-editing and by 500 basis points to 37% for classic human translation. These are changes in revenue composition, not proof of absolute growth. The report interprets the combination as failed diversification plans and renewed concentration on core services. Post-editing dominated 2025 growth intentions despite not outperforming the average in 2024. Price erosion became more visible in 2024, with freelancers expecting further declines in 2025 while companies expected relative stability.
qs: Normalising the total of all services to 100%,
2025 growth plans are dominated by post-editing, although this activity did not perform better than average in 2024.
Creative services such as content creation, transcreation and voice services show the strongest growth intentions compared to current status.

kp.d: Companies reported falling profitability, although reported gross margins remained at 38% for translation and 24% for interpreting. Staffing decreased for 39% of company respondents and increased for 11%; language departments reported decreases for 32% and increases for 10%. Neither segment expected restaffing in 2025. The report’s market-evolution scores are weighted response balances on a −2 to +2 scale, not percentage changes in economic quantities.

kp.k: Freelance sustainability and professional autonomy are deteriorating
kp.d: Only 57% of independent professionals reported earning enough from freelancing; 53% questioned their future and 23% were considering ending freelance activity. Respondents linked insecurity to lower volumes, pricing pressure and less-valued post-editing. Overall confidence in freelancing as a long-term option fell below 50%. The most junior segment’s confidence fell to 41%, but that segment represented only 3% of independent respondents. These measures concern perceived sufficiency and sustainability, not measured earnings levels or confirmed departures.
qs: It is therefore not surprising that 23% are considering ending their freelance activity.
Professionals feel trapped in a system where they cannot set boundaries due to irregular work, unstable income, and client expectations.

kp.k: Large intermediaries constrain freelancers’ bargaining power
kp.d: Freelancers reported more difficult negotiations with language companies than with direct clients, particularly over payment terms and general conditions at large language companies. Their direct-client share remained approximately 42%, against 41% previously, despite earlier plans to increase it. Company respondents reported a 69% direct-client share. Both groups intended to increase direct-client business, but the report cautions that previous intentions did not materialise.
qs: A majority of professionals indicate that it is virtually impossible to negotiate payment terms or general conditions with large language companies.
Independent language professionals report approximately the same direct client ratio as in their 2023 activity (42% vs 41%), after the substantial drop from the 45% reported a year earlier.
Whether these intentions will become reality will be seen in ELIS 2026.

kp.k: Internal departments face efficiency demands and institutional displacement
kp.d: Language departments viewed AI more positively than external providers as a means of meeting internal clients’ needs amid budget and staffing constraints. Almost half nevertheless feared that AI could weaken their organisational position. The report identifies possible bypass by internal clients and fragmented responsibility for language work: half said their department was not the sole language owner. These concerns describe internal language departments, not corporate legal departments.

kp.k: Responses emphasise traditional measures despite perceived structural disruption
kp.d: Companies primarily responded with sales and marketing, lower fixed costs and automation. The report records interest in new activities among 55%, willingness to change sector or content focus among 35%, further renegotiation with language resources among 29%, and consideration of selling among 8%. Freelancers generally planned adaptation through new skills, alternative main activities, different clients or services, and collaboration. The report recommends association-led guidance, training, networking and assistance to policymakers.

kp.k: AI roles emerge without broad organisational readiness
kp.d: Only 15% of participating companies had integrated AI-specific roles and another 15% were considering them. A majority lacked awareness of these roles or knowledge of how to integrate them. Companies were cutting support functions and concentrating on language and project-management roles, with AI the non-core recruitment exception: 25% expected AI recruitment in 2025. The report explicitly warns that recruitment intentions may not be realised.

kp.k: Training faces declining enrolment and persistent skills gaps
kp.d: Average entrants to bachelor programmes fell 13%, from 117 to 102. Interpreting and combined translation/interpreting master programmes also recorded declines, while translation masters did not. Companies remained critical of graduate preparation, particularly industry knowledge and project management; language departments were more satisfied. Students primarily preferred language roles over project-management positions, despite the report’s account of a technology-oriented industry transition.
qs: Translation technology, traditionally one of the weakest skills, has moved up a notch but industry knowledge and project management skills are still considered too weak.
Language companies, on the other hand, remain extremely critical, with the exception of source and target language skills which are considered more than average.

kp.k: AI is widespread in training but governance remains uneven
kp.d: Among students, 19% reported regular generative-AI use in their programme and 45% occasional use. Twenty teachers, 43% of those answering the question, reported formal AI-use rules, while another 20 reported none. Student predictions about machine-translation parity were divided: 42% said it would never reach human quality, whereas 38% thought it might happen before 2030. These are student expectations, not measured model performance.
qs: 19% of students indicate that they use it regularly in their programme, and 45% report occasional use.
20 teachers (43% of those who replied to the question) reported that they have formal rules in place to regulate how the technology can and should be used.
38% even thinks that this may happen before 2030, i.e. when they enter the language industry.

kp.k: Internship capacity contracts as career expectations become less optimistic
kp.d: Companies not accepting interns increased from 25% to 35%, or 62 of 179 respondents. Providers cited inadequate resources, insufficient suitable work and remote-working constraints; departments also cited regulatory or administrative barriers. Students with internship experience expressed lower market-growth and employment expectations, closer to industry respondents’ views, while remaining satisfied with their placements. Universities and hosts disagreed over formal agreements, student monitoring and compensation.
qs: The number of language companies not accepting interns increased dramatically from 25% to 35% (62 out of 179).
Students who did an internship have dramatically lower expectations regarding market growth and employment opportunities.
Virtually all students give a Satisfied score to their internship experience.
Finally, the most striking and also most controversial topic is financial compensation for interns.

kp.k: Legal translation is exposed within wider sectoral variation
kp.d: For independent professionals, the legal client sector’s reported share fell from 11% to 8%; legal and finance were among the poorest-performing sectors in 2024. Nevertheless, legal content remained the most widely handled content type among company respondents. Separately, the report cites Slator research indicating stronger performance among interpreting and audiovisual providers and flat organic growth among larger companies. It therefore does not present text-translation contraction as uniform across all language services.

With these results, ELIS 2025 results are more pessimistic than those published in the Slator 2025 Language Service Provider Index (LSPI), which showed flat organic growth among the larger language companies.

kp.k: Outsourcing remains central despite changing procurement behaviour
kp.d: Companies continued outsourcing approximately 60% of business, with a slightly increasing share going to independent professionals and only 3% operating entirely in-house, down from 5%. Departmental outsourcing varied by organisation type, and evidence of supplier consolidation was qualified by small response numbers. The proportion of department participants unwilling to outsource translation or post-editing, principally national agencies, grew from roughly 20% to 50%.
qs: Due to the wide variety of resources required, often for very small work volumes (think of long-tail languages), outsourcing has always been the main business model for the language industry.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: ELIS Research presents AI and machine translation as drivers of structural change in the language-services market, combining reduced demand and price pressure with operational efficiencies and new services.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about language services, not a study of legal practice. ELIS reports that providers attribute declining activity to technology adoption and changing procurement: clients reduce outsourcing or replace human translation with lower-priced post-editing, sometimes accepting substandard output. It also reports benefits among companies implementing AI themselves, including efficiency, lower costs and additional services; 28% report no significant impact after implementation. Post-editing rose by seven percentage points to 27% of participating companies’ revenue mix, while classic human translation also increased its share, to 37%; these are revenue shares rather than evidence that either activity grew in absolute terms. Language departments see AI as a way to manage workload under staffing and budget constraints, but fear diminished organisational standing. Respondents also envisage a split between industrial post-editing and high-quality human translation, and some anticipate renewed client appreciation of human services after disappointing AI experiences. These latter propositions are expectations, not established outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of survey respondents’ reported activity, experiences and expectations, rather than verified causal findings or model-performance benchmarks.
pts.d: ELIS 2025 gathered 1,322 responses across 50 countries: 179 language companies, 654 independent professionals, 71 language departments, 137 university staff and 281 students. Its sample primarily represents European freelancers and small and medium-sized language companies; 88% of company respondents have revenue below €5 million. Reported adoption provides context for the claimed disruption: machine translation is used in 50% of company projects and 54% of independent professionals’ work, while company AI use is reported at 34%. The report records staffing decreases among 39% of language companies and 32% of language departments, but these figures do not independently identify AI’s causal contribution. Free-text comments supply the attribution of income and workload losses to AI and post-editing. Slator research is cited as contextual evidence that larger providers experienced flatter performance and spoken-word providers fared better. No benchmark establishes translation-quality equivalence or quantifies quality degradation. ELIS expressly cautions that the survey captures opinions and expectations; market-evolution scores are weighted response balances, not percentage changes in market size.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes reported 2024 developments from 2025 expectations and longer-term beliefs about structural change and machine-translation quality.
pts.d: Reported financial, staffing and service-mix developments predominantly concern 2024; market, recruitment and business-development intentions concern 2025. Most participating companies regard the downturn as structural, although 14% expect business to return to normal and 9% attribute losses to external economic or geopolitical factors. Companies and language departments do not expect restaffing in 2025. AI roles are an exception to generally restrained company recruitment: 25% expect recruitment in this area in 2025, but the authors explicitly caution that intentions may not materialise. Only 15% of companies have integrated AI-specific roles and another 15% are considering doing so. Among students, 42% say machine translation will never reach human-translation quality, while 38% think it may happen before 2030; these are student forecasts rather than technical assessments. Benefits are qualified by actual implementation, and market consequences vary by company size, organisation type and service segment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported burdens fall particularly on freelance translators and smaller language companies, while internal language departments, students and universities face different adaptation pressures.
pts.d: Independent professionals describe reduced work volumes, income insecurity, weaker bargaining power and lower valuation of post-editing, particularly when serving large language companies. The report says 53% question their freelance future and 23% are considering leaving; those figures describe respondents’ concerns and intentions, not measured AI-caused exits. Smaller companies are more negative about AI than larger respondents, while some adopters gain efficiencies and new offerings. Internal language departments face time pressure, budget constraints and questions about their value even as they use technology to support internal clients. Universities face AI implementation challenges and reduced interest in language careers; students primarily seek traditional language roles while companies increasingly emphasise technology. The youngest freelance group’s confidence in sustainability falls to 41%, but this group accounts for only 3% of independent respondents. Interpreting and audiovisual providers are underrepresented and reportedly performed better than text-translation providers. Although the source reports weaker legal-sector translation activity and a fall in the legal sector’s share of independent professionals’ work from 11% to 8%, it does not separately establish an AI effect on legal translation or legal services.
